input:
When a pressure measurement is reported, two different questions can be asked about its quality, and keeping them apart is the starting point for understanding measurement error. The first question is how far the reading might be from the true value, and this is the province of error. In the worked figures used here, the reading is 100 units and the tolerance is 2% of reading, so the absolute error is 2 units: the reading may depart from the true value by that amount, expressed in the same units as the measurement itself. The relative error expresses the same departure as a fraction of the reading, which makes it dimensionless and allows errors on measurements of very different sizes to be compared with one another on a common basis. Error, in this sense, belongs to a particular measurement: it is the difference between the reading and the true value, even though in practice the true value is not known exactly and the error is therefore stated as a bound rather than as a known difference. Uncertainty is a different term and should not be merged with error. Uncertainty describes the range within which the value is believed to lie, together with the doubt that attaches to the measurement as a whole, taking account of the instrument and the conditions of use. A report that mixes the two terms, using error where a range is meant or uncertainty where a difference is meant, leaves the reader unable to tell what has actually been stated about the measurement.

The distinction also affects how a specification or a tolerance on an instrument should be read. A tolerance stated as a percentage, as in the worked figures, ties the permitted departure to the size of the reading, so the same instrument is held to a tighter absolute departure at a small reading than at a large one, and a reader who treats the percentage as a fixed absolute amount will misjudge the measurement at one end of the range or the other.
target:
Error in a pressure measurement is the difference between the reading and the true value. The worked figures fix the terms: the reading is 100 units, the tolerance is 2% of reading, and the absolute error is 2 units. Absolute error is expressed in the units of the measurement itself. Relative error expresses the same departure as a fraction of the reading. A relative error is dimensionless, and errors on measurements of very different sizes can be compared on that basis. Error belongs to a particular measurement. The true value is not known exactly in practice, and an error is therefore stated as a bound, not as a known difference. Uncertainty is a different term. Uncertainty describes the range within which the value is believed to lie, with the doubt that attaches to the measurement as a whole, including the instrument and the conditions of use. Error and uncertainty are not merged in careful reporting. A report that uses error where a range is meant, or uncertainty where a difference is meant, leaves the reader unable to tell what has been stated about the measurement. The distinction is practical: a bound on a difference and a range for a value lead to different uses of the same reading.

A tolerance stated as a percentage ties the permitted departure to the size of the reading. The same instrument is held to a tighter absolute departure at a small reading than at a large one. A reader who treats a percentage tolerance as a fixed absolute amount misjudges the measurement at one end of the range or the other. Relative error carries the complementary warning. A fixed absolute error is a small relative error on a large reading and a large relative error on a small reading. A single absolute figure, quoted without the reading it belongs to, does not state the quality of a measurement. Reporting practice follows from the definitions: error is reported as a difference or as a bound on a difference, and uncertainty is reported as a range.
